deep.reconstruction:
This is a printed textbook page in Fraktur, an elementary treatment of logarithms (§§111-113). It carries handwritten additions: extra decimals in the table and numbers in the margin and at the foot. Only the handwriting can be Gauss's.

(End of §111.) The book writes the logarithm to base a of y=(1+x)/(1-x) as log_a((1+x)/(1-x)) = (2/K)(x + x^3/3 + x^5/5 + ...), citing §42. Put y=a, so the left side equals 1. Then K = 2(x + x^3/3 + x^5/5 + ...). In modern terms K = ln a, the 'modulus' of the system for base a. Modern usage calls 1/ln a the modulus instead.

§112. Solve (1+x)/(1-x)=a for x: a(1-x)=1+x, so x=(a-1)/(a+1). Substituting gives K for any base. For a=10, x=9/11, and K = 2[9/11 + (1/3)(9/11)^3 + (1/5)(9/11)^5 + ...]. Summed far enough, this gives K = ln 10 = 2.3025850929...

§113. Setting K=1 gives the natural system. Its base comes from §104: a^{nω} = (1+Kω)^n. With nω=1, i.e. ω=1/n, this gives a = (1+1/n)^n. The binomial expansion is 1 + n/n + n(n-1)/(n·2n) + n(n-1)(n-2)/(n·2n·3n) + ... Letting '1 vanish against n' (i.e. n→∞) gives a = Σ 1/k! = 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + 1/24 + ...

The printed table lists 1/k! for k=1..11 to 10 decimals and sums to a = 2.71828182..., whose natural log is 1. The page then restates the series for ln((1+x)/(1-x)).

Handwritten additions (presumably by Gauss):
- He extends the decimals of the small terms: 1/5040=0.0001984126984; 1/40320=0.0000248015873016; 1/362880=0.0000027557319224 (handwritten digits roughly '31922'); 1/3628800=0.000000275573192; 1/39916800=0.0000000250521.
- Below the sum he writes 20876, 1606, 114. These are the significant digits of the next terms: 1/12! = 2.0876e-9, 1/13! = 1.606e-10, 1/14! = 1.14e-11. (Identification is mine, but certain.) He is thus pushing e beyond the printed 8 decimals.
- The struck-out figure after the sum ('1977?') is illegible. It is probably further digits of the partial sum.
- The left-margin columns (363, 274, 3014, 33154, 99462, 225228..., 2477508...1351, 'A^2') are spillover from the computation for the quantity A on the previous page. They are unrelated to this text.
errors: Printed formula for K at a=10 has misplaced brackets. It reads 2(9/11) + (1/3)(9/11)^3 + ..., but should be 2[(9/11) + (1/3)(9/11)^3 + ...]. Only the first term gets the factor 2 as printed.
Last sentence of §113 omits the logarithm sign. It should read l((1+x)/(1-x)) = 2(x + x^3/3 + ...), not (1+x)/(1-x) = ....
The denominator 11! is printed as 39908800 (as read). The correct value is 39916800; the decimal 2.505e-8 given corresponds to the correct value.
The passage from (1+1/n)^n to Σ1/k! by 'letting 1 vanish against n' is the usual non-rigorous 18th-century limit argument. The result is correct.
Using x=9/11 for ln 10 converges very slowly (ratio 81/121). It is correct but a poor computational choice. The next page computes ln 10 more efficiently via ln2+ln5.
Usage note: the book's 'modulus' K = ln a is the reciprocal of the modern modulus 1/ln a = M.

results.usually_credited_to: James Gregory (1668), Edmond Halley, standard in 18th c. texts

results.what: Handwritten extension of 1/k! decimals and the next terms 1/12!, 1/13!, 1/14! (20876, 1606, 114)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed elementary textbook on logarithms. Gauss's only contributions are routine extra decimals of 1/k! and the next few terms of the e series, plus margin arithmetic belonging to another computation.

checkable.asserts: The series with x=9/11 sums to ln 10 = 2.3025850929...
Correct value of 11!; the printed 39908800 is a misprint
The bottom figures 20876, 1606, 114 are the digits of 2.0876e-9, 1.606e-10, 1.14e-11
Partial sum through 1/11! = 2.71828182619..., consistent with the printed 2.71828182...

transcription_corrections: The last line of the §113 text should read l((1+x)/(1-x)) = 2(x + x^3/3 + ...); the 'l' is missing in the print itself.
Handwritten digits after 1/362880 are likely '31922' (correct continuation 0.0000027557319224), not '319722'.
The bottom numbers 20876 / 1606 / 114 are handwritten digits of 1/12!, 1/13!, 1/14!, not page references.
The left-margin numbers are spillover of the previous page's computation, not part of this page's content.
